units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Citizenship Education
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Citizenship education develops the knowledge, values and practical skills people need to participate responsibly in public life. It helps learners understand citizenship, how public institutions operate, how rights are protected, and why duties such as obeying lawful rules and respecting other people matter. It is not simply memorising government facts: students should apply civic principles to everyday decisions at home, school and in the wider community. A citizen is a person recognised by a state as belonging to it under that state's law. Citizenship may be acquired through routes recognised by the constitution and legislation, such as birth, registration or naturalisation, subject to applicable conditions. Citizenship is distinct from residence: a person may live in a country without being its citizen. Citizenship education supports peaceful coexistence by teaching respect for diversity, constitutional values, tolerance, accountability and informed participation. Rights and responsibilities should be taught together: exercising a right does not permit a person to violate another person's rights.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Duties and Obligations of Citizens
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: A duty or obligation is a responsibility a person is expected or legally required to perform. Citizens' obligations help a society function fairly and safely. They include obeying valid laws, respecting the rights of others, paying taxes when legally liable, participating in elections when eligible, protecting public property, and contributing to community life. Civic duties are often grouped into political, economic and social responsibilities. Political responsibilities include informed voting by eligible citizens, lawful participation in public affairs and respect for constitutional institutions. Economic responsibilities include paying taxes and complying with lawful financial obligations. Social responsibilities include respecting others, protecting public facilities, assisting community initiatives and promoting peaceful relations. Age and legal capacity matter. A student below voting age is not expected to vote, but can still learn about public issues, respect others' rights and contribute to school or community activities. Duties must be carried out lawfully: citizens do not acquire general police powers merely because they have a responsibility to support public safety.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Promotion of Our Traditions and Customs
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Customs are shared practices and accepted ways of behaving within a community. Traditions are beliefs, ceremonies, knowledge and practices transmitted across generations. They may include language, music, dance, dress, food, crafts, festivals, oral history and forms of community organisation. Cultural heritage contributes to identity and can help people understand their history and maintain social bonds. It can be promoted through teaching local languages, documenting oral histories, supporting museums and cultural centres, encouraging responsible festivals, preserving traditional arts and crafts, and including accurate cultural studies in education. Families and community elders can pass on knowledge, while schools, media and public institutions can create opportunities for different communities to share their heritage respectfully. Nigeria is culturally diverse. Promotion of one community's heritage should not imply that other groups are inferior or that every person from a group follows the same practice. Cultural practices also need to be assessed against constitutional rights, dignity, equality and safety.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: National Consciousness, Integrity and Unity
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: National consciousness is awareness of belonging to a country and an informed concern for its wellbeing. It involves understanding national symbols, history, institutions, constitutional principles and shared responsibilities. National unity is the willingness of people from different communities to live and work together as members of one political society while respecting their differences. Integrity means acting honestly and consistently with sound ethical principles, including when there is no immediate reward. In public life, integrity requires truthful communication, fair treatment, responsible use of public resources and refusal to abuse entrusted authority. Unity is not the absence of disagreement; citizens can debate policies while remaining committed to lawful and peaceful ways of resolving differences. National consciousness can be strengthened by civic education, inclusive public institutions, respect for the constitution, fair access to opportunity, responsible leadership, inter-community cooperation and accurate knowledge of national history.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Capitalist Democracy
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Democracy is a system of government in which public authority is derived from the people and exercised through constitutional institutions. In a representative democracy, citizens choose representatives through periodic elections. Essential features include political participation, genuine electoral choice, the rule of law, protection of fundamental rights, accountability, public debate and peaceful transfer of power. Capitalism is an economic system in which productive assets may be privately owned and economic activity is substantially organised through markets, investment and exchange. A capitalist democracy combines democratic political institutions with an economy in which private enterprise and market activity play a major role. The political and economic systems are related but not identical: holding elections does not automatically guarantee fair economic opportunity, and private ownership does not itself guarantee democratic government. A democratic state sets legal rules for economic activity, protects lawful property rights, regulates markets where necessary and remains responsible for public goods and social protection.

units.body: A political party is an organised association of people who share broad political goals and seek to influence or control government through constitutional political processes, especially elections. Parties develop policy programmes, select or support candidates, campaign, mobilise voters and organise elected representatives. They connect citizens' concerns with public decision-making. Political parties differ from pressure groups. A party normally seeks elected office and responsibility for governing, while a pressure group seeks to influence policy without necessarily contesting elections to form a government. Civil society organisations may monitor public institutions, provide services or advocate for causes; they are not automatically political parties. In a democratic system, parties can present alternative programmes, recruit leaders, educate voters, aggregate interests and provide opposition scrutiny. Healthy party competition requires internal organisation, transparent candidate selection, lawful campaign finance, peaceful conduct and respect for electoral outcomes.

units.title: Poverty and Its Effects
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.

units.body: Poverty is a condition in which people lack sufficient resources to meet essential needs and participate adequately in society. It may involve inadequate income, food insecurity, unsafe housing, limited access to education and healthcare, insecure work or exclusion from essential services. Poverty is multidimensional: two households with similar income may face different levels of hardship because of health, location, household size or access to public services. Poverty can contribute to malnutrition, preventable illness, interrupted schooling, unsafe living conditions and reduced opportunities. It can increase vulnerability to exploitation and make it harder for people to participate in community and political life. These effects are shaped by employment opportunities, public infrastructure, economic conditions, education, health and social protection. Responses include access to quality education, decent work, skills development, reliable infrastructure, effective public services, fair economic opportunities and targeted support for vulnerable households.

objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.

units.body: Political apathy is a lack of interest in or willingness to participate in political processes. It may appear as failure to register where eligible, refusal to vote, avoidance of public discussion or disengagement from civic organisations. It should not be confused with lawful criticism: a citizen who questions a candidate or rejects a policy is still engaging with public affairs. Factors associated with political apathy can include distrust caused by unfulfilled promises, perceived electoral malpractice, political violence, intimidation, lack of accessible information, poverty, exclusion and the belief that participation will not make a difference. Some people face practical barriers such as disability access, distance from polling facilities or work obligations. Measures to reduce apathy include credible and impartial election administration, accessible civic education, transparent public decisions, safe participation, accountability for misconduct, inclusive consultation and peaceful political competition.

objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.

units.body: Leaders are entrusted with authority to make decisions and act on behalf of a group or community. They fail to protect followers' interests when they place personal advantage, private networks or party interests above public responsibilities. Other contributing factors may include weak institutions, poor access to information, lack of transparency, conflicts of interest, intimidation of critics and ineffective oversight. Good leadership requires honesty, competence, fairness, consultation, respect for rights and willingness to explain decisions. Leaders should use public resources for authorised purposes, disclose relevant conflicts, listen to affected communities and apply rules consistently. Accountability can be strengthened through independent oversight, transparent budgets, credible elections, access to public information, legislative scrutiny, judicial review and lawful complaint mechanisms. These safeguards do not guarantee perfect leadership, but they make abuse more difficult to conceal and easier to challenge.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Popular Participation
objectives: Explain the source topic of popular participation and its relevance to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body:
POPULAR PARTICIPATION

Popular participation means the active and informed involvement of people in decisions and activities that affect public life. It is important to democracy because government is more responsive when citizens can express concerns, choose representatives, scrutinise public decisions and contribute to community development. Participation can occur through voting by eligible citizens, public consultations, community meetings, petitions, lawful advocacy, peaceful demonstrations, civic associations and service projects.

Participation should be informed, inclusive and peaceful. People should seek reliable information, respect the rights of others and use lawful channels. A person who disagrees with a policy can still participate constructively by asking questions, presenting evidence or proposing alternatives. Participation is not limited to election day; it continues between elections through public discussion and accountability.

Barriers may include lack of information, intimidation, inaccessible meetings, poverty, discrimination and distrust of institutions. Public authorities can encourage participation by making information accessible, protecting lawful expression, consulting affected groups and explaining how public feedback is used. In examination answers, define participation and connect each example to the way it gives citizens a voice.

units.title: Formation of Popular Organisations
objectives: Explain the source topic of formation of popular organisations and its relevance to responsible citizenship.

units.body:
FORMATION OF POPULAR ORGANISATIONS

Popular organisations are associations formed by people who share interests or seek to address public concerns. Examples include political parties, pressure groups, trade associations, professional bodies, youth organisations and community development associations. They help people organise their views, cooperate on common goals and communicate with public institutions.

An organisation is usually formed after people identify a shared concern, discuss their objectives and agree on rules. They may establish membership requirements, select leaders, create committees, decide how meetings will be held, identify lawful sources of funding and register with the relevant authority where registration is required. A written constitution or set of rules can explain the organisation's name, aims, membership, leadership, decision-making process and accountability arrangements.

Different organisations have different purposes. Political parties seek electoral office and responsibility for government. Pressure groups seek to influence policies without necessarily forming a government. Community associations may focus on local services or development. Effective organisations are transparent, democratic in their internal processes, peaceful and accountable to members. They should not use threats or violence to advance their objectives.

units.body:
HUMAN RIGHTS

Human rights are basic entitlements and freedoms that belong to people because they are human. They protect dignity and help individuals live safely and participate in society. In Nigeria, constitutional protections include rights relating to life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing, private and family life, freedom of thought and expression, peaceful assembly and association, movement, and freedom from discrimination, subject to the Constitution and applicable law.

Rights are accompanied by responsibilities to respect the rights of others. Some rights may be subject to lawful limitations in defined circumstances; this does not give officials unlimited power to disregard them. A restriction must have a lawful basis and be applied consistently with constitutional safeguards. Students should distinguish a right from a privilege granted at someone's discretion.

Where a person's rights may have been violated, appropriate responses include documenting relevant facts, seeking trusted legal or institutional advice, using complaint mechanisms and approaching competent authorities or courts. Do not encourage retaliation or vigilantism. For examination answers, state the meaning of human rights, identify examples accurately and explain how each protects dignity or freedom.

units.body:
EMERGENCY

An emergency is a serious and unexpected situation that requires prompt action to protect life, health, property or the environment. Emergencies may arise from fires, road crashes, flooding, building collapse, severe illness, violence or other dangerous events. The correct response depends on the nature of the incident and the instructions of trained responders.

Preparedness reduces harm. Individuals and institutions can identify safe exits, know how to contact emergency services, keep essential information accessible, learn basic first-aid principles from qualified providers and practise evacuation procedures. During an emergency, people should protect themselves from immediate danger, alert the appropriate emergency service, give clear and truthful information, follow official instructions and avoid spreading unverified messages.

Do not enter unsafe buildings, touch dangerous substances or attempt rescues beyond your training. After the immediate danger has passed, affected people may need medical attention, shelter, counselling or help from public agencies and community organisations. units.body:
DRUG USE AND ABUSE I

A drug is a substance that can affect the way the body or mind functions. Medicines are drugs used to prevent, diagnose or treat health conditions. When medicines are prescribed or supplied by an authorised professional, they should be used according to the directions on the label or prescription. Taking a medicine in a different dose, using another person's prescription or combining substances without professional advice can be dangerous.

Drug misuse or abuse refers to harmful or non-medical use of a substance, including use in ways that increase health and social risks. Some substances affect the central nervous system, mood, judgement or behaviour. Legal status differs between substances and jurisdictions, but legality alone does not make a substance safe. Alcohol and tobacco, for example, can also cause harm.

Students should avoid experimenting with unknown substances and should not share medicines. If someone may have taken a harmful substance, seek urgent medical help and give responders accurate information. Do not shame or stigmatise the person. Health problems require appropriate professional assessment, not punishment or unsupported home remedies.

DRUG ABUSE II: RISK FACTORS AND CAUSES

Harmful substance use rarely has a single cause. Risk factors can include peer pressure, curiosity, stress, trauma, misinformation, easy availability, family or community influences, untreated health conditions and the belief that a substance will solve a problem. These factors do not mean that every person exposed to them will misuse drugs, and they should not be used to label or blame individuals.

Protective factors include accurate health education, supportive relationships, access to trusted adults and health professionals, positive activities, safe communities and early help when a person is struggling. Young people can practise refusal skills, leave unsafe situations, question misleading claims and seek help without fear of humiliation.

Self-medication is risky because symptoms may have different causes and medicines can interact or cause side effects. Only use medicines as directed by a qualified professional. In examination answers, separate possible causes from effects and prevention. Use non-stigmatising language: a person experiencing substance-related harm needs safety, treatment and support.

units.body:
EFFECTS OF DRUG ABUSE

Harmful drug use can affect physical health, mental wellbeing, learning, relationships and community safety. Possible effects depend on the substance, amount, frequency, the person's health and whether substances are combined. They can include impaired judgement and coordination, accidents, dependence, anxiety, sleep problems, damage to body organs, financial difficulties and disruption to school or work.

Substance-related harm can affect families through conflict, worry, loss of trust and financial strain. Communities may experience increased health-service needs, unsafe behaviour and reduced productivity. These outcomes are not inevitable for every person and should not be used to stigmatise people who need help. Dependence is a health concern and may require professional treatment and ongoing support.

Prevention and early intervention are more effective when they combine education, supportive relationships, accessible health services and proportionate enforcement against illegal supply. If an overdose or serious reaction is suspected, contact emergency medical services immediately. Do not wait for symptoms to disappear or rely on unverified remedies. In examinations, explain each effect rather than listing vague claims.

PREVENTION OF DRUG ABUSE

Preventing harmful substance use requires action by individuals, families, schools, health services, communities and government. Individuals can learn accurate health information, avoid unknown substances, follow medicine instructions, develop refusal skills, choose supportive peer groups and seek help when facing pressure or distress. They should not share prescription medicines or encourage others to experiment.

Parents and caregivers can maintain open communication, model safe behaviour, notice changes without jumping to conclusions and seek professional advice when concerned. Schools can provide age-appropriate education, counselling referrals and safe activities. Health professionals can offer confidential assessment and treatment within applicable rules. Community organisations can support young people and reduce stigma.

Public agencies can regulate medicines, prevent illegal supply, support treatment services and communicate risks clearly. Prevention should not rely only on punishment: people experiencing dependence need access to health care and social support. In examination answers, group measures by individual, family, school, community and government, then explain how each reduces risk.

ACTIVITIES OF DRUG LAW ENFORCEMENT AGENCIES

Drug law enforcement agencies help protect the public by implementing laws relating to controlled substances and illegal drug supply. In Nigeria, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has a central role in preventing and investigating drug trafficking and related offences, while other public bodies have distinct responsibilities in border control, medicines regulation, policing, public health and education.

Activities may include intelligence gathering within legal limits, investigation of suspected offences, lawful seizure of prohibited substances, prosecution through the proper legal process, public education, cooperation with other agencies and support for prevention and treatment initiatives. Agencies must respect due process, human rights and rules governing evidence. Enforcement is not a licence for arbitrary searches, detention or punishment.

Effective drug control combines lawful enforcement with prevention, accurate information, treatment and rehabilitation. Agencies should coordinate rather than duplicate or confuse their mandates. In examination answers, identify the agency's public purpose and describe its activities accurately. Do not claim that every health or education activity is performed by the NDLEA alone.

units.body:
RESPONSIBLE PARENTHOOD

Responsible parenthood is the commitment and ability of parents or caregivers to meet children's needs and support their healthy development. These needs include food, shelter, healthcare, education, protection, emotional support, guidance and opportunities to develop social skills. Parenthood involves long-term responsibilities, not only providing money or meeting a child's immediate physical needs.

Parents and caregivers should create a safe environment, listen to children, set appropriate boundaries, provide positive examples and protect children from neglect, abuse and exploitation. Care should be shared fairly and should recognise the child's age, abilities and individual needs. Children should be treated with dignity and their views considered in matters affecting them, in ways appropriate to their maturity.

Responsible parenthood also includes seeking healthcare, supporting education, teaching respect and helping children learn independence. No family is identical, and economic hardship should not be used to shame parents who need support. Public services and communities can help families access health, education and social protection. In examination answers, explain the broad dimensions of care and give practical examples.

FACTORS THAT SUPPORT SUCCESSFUL RESPONSIBLE PARENTHOOD

Responsible parenthood is more likely to succeed when caregivers have supportive relationships, accurate information and access to essential services. Helpful factors include effective communication between caregivers, shared planning and decision-making, emotional maturity, patience, stable and safe living conditions, access to healthcare, education, adequate resources and positive role modelling.

Parents should agree on consistent and age-appropriate expectations, resolve disagreements without violence and make time to listen to children. They should seek professional advice about health, learning or behavioural concerns rather than relying on harmful myths. Family planning and preparation for caregiving can help adults consider their responsibilities and available support.

No single factor guarantees success. Families may face unemployment, illness or other pressures and may need help from relatives, schools, health services and community organisations. The child's safety and dignity remain central. In examination answers, list relevant factors and explain how each supports the child's physical, emotional, educational or social development.

units.body:
TRAFFIC REGULATIONS

Traffic regulations are laws and rules that guide road users and the movement of vehicles to reduce danger and maintain orderly transport. They apply to drivers, motorcyclists, cyclists, passengers and pedestrians. Regulations may cover licensing, vehicle roadworthiness, speed limits, traffic signs and signals, lane use, overtaking, seat belts, helmets, parking and pedestrian crossings.

Road signs and traffic lights communicate instructions and warnings. Drivers must understand and obey them, maintain safe distances and give appropriate priority to vulnerable road users. Pedestrians should use safe crossing points where available, remain alert and avoid sudden movement into traffic. Passengers should use available safety restraints and avoid distracting the driver.

Traffic rules protect life and help prevent collisions, congestion and damage to property. Enforcement should be lawful, fair and consistent, while road authorities should provide clear signs and safe infrastructure. In examination answers, define traffic regulations and connect examples to the safety purpose they serve.

units.body:
WAYS OF REDUCING ROAD ACCIDENTS

Road accidents can be reduced through safer behaviour, roadworthy vehicles, effective infrastructure and consistent enforcement. Drivers should obey speed limits, avoid driving while impaired or dangerously tired, maintain safe following distances, use seat belts and avoid distractions such as handling a phone while driving. Motorcyclists should use approved helmets and follow traffic rules.

Vehicles should be inspected and maintained, with particular attention to brakes, tyres, lights and steering. Pedestrians should use safe crossings, remain visible and avoid distractions near moving traffic. Road authorities can maintain roads, improve lighting, mark lanes, provide signs and crossings, identify dangerous locations and respond to hazards.

Road safety is a shared responsibility. Accidents may still occur despite care, so emergency response and prompt medical assistance are important. Do not assume that every crash is caused by one person; investigations should establish the facts. In examination answers, group prevention measures under drivers, pedestrians, vehicle owners and government, and explain the risk each measure reduces.

ROLES OF INDIVIDUALS AND GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING TRAFFIC REGULATIONS

Individuals help maintain traffic regulations by obeying road signs and signals, using seat belts and helmets, keeping vehicles roadworthy, avoiding impaired or distracted driving, respecting pedestrians and reporting dangerous road conditions through appropriate channels. Passengers should avoid distracting drivers and should use safety restraints where provided. Pedestrians should use safe crossing points and remain alert.

Government responsibilities include making and updating traffic laws, maintaining roads, installing visible signs and signals, providing pedestrian facilities, licensing drivers and vehicles, educating the public, investigating crashes and enforcing regulations fairly. Emergency and health services also play a role in responding to road injuries.

Road safety improves when individual conduct and public infrastructure work together. Enforcement alone cannot compensate for unsafe roads, poor signs or defective vehicles; equally, good infrastructure cannot prevent every collision if road users ignore safety rules. In examination answers, separate individual responsibilities from government responsibilities and explain their combined effect.

units.body:
INTERPERSONAL RELATIONSHIPS

An interpersonal relationship is a connection or interaction between two or more people. Such relationships occur among family members, friends, classmates, colleagues and neighbours. Healthy relationships are built on respect, honesty, empathy, trust, communication, cooperation and appropriate boundaries.

Good communication involves listening carefully, expressing concerns clearly and avoiding insults or threats. Empathy means trying to understand another person's feelings and perspective without assuming that both people must agree. Trust develops when people keep reasonable commitments and act consistently. Boundaries help people understand personal space, privacy and acceptable conduct.

Disagreements are normal, but they should be handled peacefully through discussion, apology where appropriate, compromise or help from a trusted mediator. Violence, coercion, harassment and humiliation are not signs of a healthy relationship. In examination answers, define the concept, identify qualities of positive relationships and explain how they support cooperation and wellbeing.

units.body:
INTER-COMMUNAL RELATIONSHIPS

Inter-communal relationships are the interactions and connections between different communities. Communities may cooperate through trade, shared services, cultural events, education, intermarriage, sports, environmental projects and local development. Positive relationships encourage mutual understanding, trust, peaceful coexistence and the exchange of skills and resources.

Differences in language, customs, land use, resources or political interests can sometimes create tension. Such differences should be addressed through fair communication and lawful institutions rather than stereotypes or collective blame. Community leaders, youth groups, women’s organisations, schools and public authorities can create opportunities for dialogue and joint projects.

Respectful cooperation does not require communities to abandon their identities. Each community can preserve its culture while recognising the dignity and rights of others. In examination answers, explain both the benefits of cooperation and the importance of resolving disagreements peacefully. Use examples that show practical interaction rather than simply stating that communities should love one another.

units.body:
SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES IN INTER-COMMUNAL SOCIETIES

Disputes between communities may arise from disagreements about land, boundaries, resources, leadership, trade or misunderstandings. Peaceful settlement aims to establish facts, address legitimate concerns and prevent further harm. Violence and collective punishment deepen conflict and should not be treated as acceptable methods of resolution.

Methods include dialogue, negotiation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration where appropriate, lawful customary processes and formal court proceedings. Dialogue allows parties to explain their concerns. Negotiation involves parties seeking an agreement directly. Mediation uses a neutral person to help them communicate and explore options. Arbitration involves an agreed decision-maker, while courts determine legal disputes under the law.

A fair process should hear all affected parties, respect rights, avoid intimidation and record any agreement clearly. Serious offences and threats should be referred to competent authorities. In examination answers, distinguish the methods and explain when a neutral mediator or lawful institution can help restore peaceful relations.
